Quality Models and the Quality Tree

Why quality shapes structure

Learning objective — Explain why quality goals, more than features, decide an architecture.

Core principle

Two systems with the same features can need completely different structures because their quality goals differ.

Evidence from the field

arc42 section 10 states the motivation directly: quality requirements strongly shape architecture, so the important ones must be identified specifically and measurably. The few most important belong in section 1.2; section 10 holds the full set.

Engineering response

Before choosing any structure, write down the three to five qualities that matter most for this system.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Name one feature two systems could share and one quality goal that would make their architectures differ.

Quality Models and the Quality Tree

Use a model as a checklist

Learning objective — Use a published quality model to avoid forgetting a quality.

Core principle

A quality model is a checklist, not a goal list. You pick from it; you do not satisfy all of it.

Evidence from the field

ISO/IEC 25010:2023 describes a product quality model of nine characteristics, each divided into subcharacteristics. arc42 cites it as a basis for grouping and as a thoroughness checklist. The Q42 quality model (quality.arc42.org, CC BY-SA 4.0) lists 191 quality characteristics, 150 example requirements and 56 solution approaches.

Engineering response

Scan a model once to find qualities you had not considered, then keep only the few that matter.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is trying to satisfy every characteristic in a quality model a mistake?

Quality Models and the Quality Tree

Build a quality tree

Learning objective — Refine one quality into leaves you can attach a scenario to.

Core principle

A quality tree breaks a vague word into specific concerns, ending in leaves that can each carry a measurable scenario.

Evidence from the field

arc42 calls this a quality attribute tree and notes that Bass and colleagues call it the quality attribute utility tree. Example: Performance → response time → checkout under peak load; Performance → throughput → orders per minute at lunchtime.

Engineering response

Stop splitting when a leaf is specific enough that you could write a test for it.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Is "the system should be fast" a leaf? What would you change to make it one?

Quality Models and the Quality Tree

Rank the leaves

Learning objective — Rank leaves by importance to the business and difficulty for the architecture.

Core principle

Not every leaf deserves equal effort. Rank by business importance and by how hard it is to achieve.

Evidence from the field

A simple two-letter grade works: H, M or L for importance and for difficulty. Leaves that are High and High are your architecture drivers; leaves that are High and Low are just good practice.

Engineering response

Put your High/High leaves at the top of section 10 and make sure each has at least one scenario.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which leaves most deserve a decision record: High/High, or Low/Low?

titles: Use a model as a checklist

quiz.q: What is the best use of a published quality model such as ISO/IEC 25010 or Q42?
o: Use it as a checklist to find qualities you may have missed, then keep only the few that matter.
Skip it, because models are too general to help.
quiz.why: The models are prompts. arc42 itself cites ISO 25010 as a basis for grouping and as a thoroughness checklist.

quiz.q: Which is a leaf of a quality tree?
o: Checkout responds quickly at lunchtime peak
quiz.why: A leaf is specific enough that a scenario and a test can be written for it.

quiz.q: Which leaves are the architecture drivers?
quiz.why: High/High leaves are important to the business and hard to achieve, so they shape structure.

ps: A quality tree is the first Level 2 artefact because it forces the conversation most teams skip: what do we actually care about, and in what order? Start from the three to five quality goals in section 1.2 of your arc42 and give each a branch. Then split each branch until its leaves are things you could test.

Use the published models as a prompt, not a template. Read the ISO 25010 characteristics and the Q42 list once, ask "does this matter here?", and cross out most of them. A tree with eight leaves that the team believes beats one with eighty it has never read.

Illustrative case. A small team builds an ordering app for street-food vendors. Their first list of qualities has fourteen adjectives. In a one-hour session they cross out all but five and build a tree: Performance (checkout stays fast at lunchtime), Availability (orders still work when mobile data is weak), Security (card data never touches our servers), Modifiability (a new vendor can be added without code changes) and Cost (hosting under US$200 a month). They rank each leaf H/M/L twice. Only "orders work with weak connectivity" is High on both. That single leaf drives their biggest decision, an offline-first design.
Mark your own work against these four criteria. Score each 0, 1 or 2.
head: Criterion
0: Missing
1: Partial
2: Competent
rows: Every leaf could carry a measurable scenario
Importance and difficulty ranked for every leaf
More than fifteen leaves, none prioritised
A short list with the High/High leaves named
Names which part of the current design is most at risk
